title: Jealous of a conch
hookLine: Andal questions Vishnu's conch about his lips: why bhakti longs to be near God, and why the conch sounds at worship
carry: bhakti longs to be near god
last: WHAT'S OFFERED TO GOD IS SET APART.

lines: CAMPHOR? THE LOTUS? IS IT SWEET?
cards: Does it smell of camphor? Of the lotus? Is it sweet?
A young woman is asking, urgently, and she's asking a seashell. Not any shell: the white conch that rests in the hand of Vishnu, and that Krishna lifts to his lips and blows.
She wants to know what his mouth is like, and the conch is the only one who'd know. It's Andal again, in the seventh song of the Nachiyar Tirumoli, and she's jealous of a shell.

teach.b: The opening, in paraphrase: does it smell of camphor, of the lotus, does his coral mouth taste sweet? I long to know.
Tell me, white conch of the deep sea, what is the scent and taste of the lips of the one who broke the elephant's tusk? Then the questions turn into complaints.

teach.h: THE CONCH IN THE LORD'S HAND
teach.b: You were born in the ocean, she tells the conch, and now you live in his hand. You rest on his mouth while the rest of us wait. Others can only stand and look at him from afar, and you, a shell, go right up to his lips.
It's a love poem, and a funny one: she's envying an object. So why a conch? In the Bhagavad Gita, before the battle, Krishna blows his conch, named Panchajanya.
For a Vaishnava listener, the conch isn't decoration. It's one of the Lord's own emblems, held in his hand, carrying his breath.

teach.h: WHY THE CONCH SOUNDS AT WORSHIP
teach.b: That's why, in many homes and temples, a conch is still blown as worship begins. Now the teaching. Bhakti, loving devotion, isn't content to admire God from far off.
It wants to be near. Sri Vaishnava teachers read the conch as a picture of the devotee the Lord keeps closest, so Andal's envy is also a prayer: let me be that close, let my life carry your breath.
And the tradition didn't clean her up. It kept a young woman's longing, plain and bodily, taste and scent and jealousy, as a way of talking about God.

how: Sri Vaishnava Hindus recite Andal's Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes, and in Vishnu worship the conch is blown and held as one of the Lord's own emblems.

s: Andal questions a conch shell about the scent of the Lord's lips
camphor, the lotus, sweetness: she asks the white conch, because it would know.
the tradition cut the bodily language out of Andal's verses
it kept the taste, the scent and the jealousy, and recites them as scripture.
in many Hindu homes and temples, a conch is blown as worship begins
it's one of the Lord's own emblems. in the Gita, Krishna's conch even has a name: Panchajanya.

games.q: you're Andal, longing to know what the Lord is like up close. you can't ask him. whom do you ask?
o: the white conch in his hand.
your friends from the dawn vow.
games.why: she asks the conch, because it rests on his lips, and then she envies it for being so close.

practice: In many Hindu homes a conch is blown at the start of evening worship: one long breath sent through a shell. You don't need one.
Breathe in slowly, and on a long breath out, imagine the sound moving through you the way breath moves through the conch. Do it three times. If you pray, let the last breath carry a name of God.
If you don't, let it carry a name you love.
